parakeet: One of the hardest realizations I had during deconstruction was this. I accepted something as true before it was ever demonstrated as true. Not because I had evidence, not because I understood the mechanics, but because someone else was confident about it. Someone else's confidence literally became my certainty. And once I realized that, the entire structure collapsed. When I deconverted, I had to confront some very uncomfortable truths. I wasn't just wrong about religion. I had accepted an entire worldview based on anecdotal testimony, emotional experiences, and my own ignorance of how those experiences actually worked. I had mistaken not understanding something for evidence that something supernatural was happening. My deconversion wasn't just about losing faith. It was about realizing that I had been cheating at knowledge. I realized I had accepted a reality as true before it had ever been demonstrated as true. I let my ignorance of the mechanics be fueled by the volume of testimony. And that realization forced me to make a commitment. And here's the uncomfortable part. This isn't just a religion problem. This pattern shows up everywhere. Our politics, culture wars, social media, common knowledge. We constantly inherit beliefs we've never investigated. We repeat things we've never verified. We share ideas we've never tested. What we call common knowledge is often just borrowed certainty. We treat common knowledge as a safety net, but it's often just a consensus of people who also don't know how the thing works.
